title: 2026: The Year of Agents in Legal AI
author: Adrian Parlow · Ryan Wilson

dom.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Legora agrees that AI will fundamentally reconfigure legal workflows and acknowledges reliability and legal-team trust as necessary. However, its central prediction that AI will perform end-to-end legal work in 2026 goes beyond—and partly conflicts with—the cluster’s evidence-based emphasis on bounded, supervised tasks rather than near-term general legal autonomy.
qs: Both our teams share the same vision of the future: AI performing end-to-end legal work.
Below we break down what that transformation actually means, how the technology has finally caught up with our vision, and what it takes to build it in a way that legal teams can trust.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: The source supports the shift from answer generation to adaptive, multistep task execution and agrees that legal deployment requires human oversight, governance, matter context and traceability. It is more promotional and optimistic than the cluster: it asserts safe end-to-end capability without measured evidence and does not substantively examine error propagation or whether verification becomes the economic bottleneck.
qs: Rather than following a predetermined path, the agent assesses what it knows, decides what to do next, executes it, evaluates the result, and iterates — pulling in the right skills and context as the work demands.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source supports the shift from isolated chatbot answers to planned, multi-step legal workflows and explicitly retains human oversight and context. Its stronger prediction of reliable end-to-end execution is speculative and under-evidenced, but it does not reject the cluster’s emphasis on connected workflows and human checkpoints.
qs: An agent receives a task, creates a plan of action, executes the plan, and returns a result.
In 2026, it means agents completing complex, end-to-end legal work — autonomously, in context, with human oversight built in.

st.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s broader proposition that competition is shifting toward control of end-to-end legal workflows. Legora’s integration with Walter AI also fits the supplier–partner structure described in the synthesis. However, it offers forecasts and software-development analogies rather than evidence of realised legal-workflow displacement, and does not establish whether foundation-model providers will supersede specialist vendors.
qs: We're incredibly excited about the partnership and have already started working together on building the next generation of legal technology for our customers.
Both our teams share the same vision of the future: AI performing end-to-end legal work.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that AI will reshape how legal work is performed rather than merely improve isolated tasks. It specifically forecasts autonomous, end-to-end execution with human oversight, but offers a product-led prediction based mainly on analogy to software agents and does not substantively address shifts among legal departments, ALSPs and firms, pricing change, or demonstrated market-wide returns.
qs: Similar to the arrival of the internet, which reshaped how people connected and how virtually every industry operated, agentic AI will fundamentally reshape how legal work gets done.
In 2026, it means agents completing complex, end-to-end legal work — autonomously, in context, with human oversight built in.

kp.k: Authors predict end-to-end legal agents in 2026
kp.d: In this March 11, 2026 product update, Adrian Parlow and Ryan Wilson assert that legal AI is progressing from simple prompts and document Q&A in 2023, through advanced multi-step workflows in 2025, to autonomous end-to-end work with human oversight in 2026. This is the authors' forecast and capability claim, rather than a reported legal deployment study.
qs: Both our teams share the same vision of the future: AI performing end-to-end legal work.
2026 is the year that vision becomes reality.

In 2023, legal AI meant simple prompts and basic document Q&A. By 2025, it meant advanced multi-step workflows. In 2026, it means agents completing complex, end-to-end legal work — autonomously, in context, with human oversight built in.

kp.k: Software development provides the analogy for legal transformation
kp.d: The authors describe software AI progressing from line completion in 2021 to file editing in 2023 and multi-hour autonomous tasks in 2025, followed by multi-day projects. They identify Claude Opus 4.5 as a capability inflection point and claim AI can more reliably complete engineering tasks requiring 12 human hours. They use this trajectory to argue that legal work follows one cycle behind; the supplied text includes source markers but no underlying study details.
qs: In 2021, GitHub Copilot could autocomplete a line of code. By 2023, Cursor was editing entire files. By 2025, Claude Code was completing multi-hour tasks autonomously.
Today, AI agents in software are running multi-day projects spanning millions of lines of code across thousands of files, and largely getting it right.
AI can now more reliably complete software engineering tasks that are more complex, more demanding, and would take a human 12 hours to complete, and it's continuing to improve.
Legal is tracking the same curve as software development, one cycle behind.

kp.k: Shared task structures underpin transfer from software to law
kp.d: The authors argue that precision-sensitive text, reusable patterns, version control, collaboration, costly errors and large contextual records make legal work structurally similar to software development. Their broader framework describes information work as reading, thinking, writing and verifying, applying it both to associate contract review and engineering. This is an analogy supporting their transfer argument, not a comparative empirical finding.
qs: Both are dominated by text where precision determines outcomes.
Both rely on reusable templates and established patterns—code libraries and clause libraries aren't so different.
Both have near zero tolerance for errors, where small mistakes carry outsized consequences.
READ (ingest unstructured information)
THINK (apply domain knowledge)
WRITE (produce structured output)
VERIFY (check against standards)
This sequence describes an associate working through a contract review just as accurately as it describes an engineer refactoring a codebase.

kp.k: Agents execute adaptively rather than answer or follow scripts
kp.d: The authors distinguish assistive chatbots from agents that plan and execute tasks, and reject describing fixed chained workflows as genuine agency. Their defining mechanism is an iterative loop of reasoning, action and evaluation that selects context and skills as needed. Evaluation here is the agent's assessment of intermediate results, distinct from the human approval checkpoints discussed elsewhere.
qs: A chatbot receives a question and provides an answer. It's assistive technology. It helps you work.
An agent receives a task, creates a plan of action, executes the plan, and returns a result. It's execution technology. It does the work, end-to-end.

Some vendors market their tools as "agentic" today, but the truth is they are better described as chained workflows—a fixed sequence of steps defined in advance, where each prompt feeds into the next.
What makes it agentic is the agent loop: a continuous cycle of reasoning, action, and evaluation that runs until a task is complete.

kp.k: Matter-wide context and memory expand claimed agent capabilities
kp.d: The authors identify long-context processing and persistent memory as capabilities enabling agents to work across entire matter files and retain drafting styles, prior positions and client preferences across sessions. They claim exhaustive review beyond human-team scale and increasingly tailored work, without supplying measurements of review completeness or personalization.
qs: Long-context: agents can read and work across an entire matter file at once, not just a single document, unlocking exhaustive review at a scale no human team can match.
Memory-driven: agents that remember prior positions, preferred drafting styles, and client preferences across sessions, getting smarter and more tailored the more they're used.

kp.k: Execution shifts from suggestions to completed legal deliverables
kp.d: The authors envisage agents redlining documents, executing research, incorporating findings and producing diligence reports rather than merely suggesting actions or identifying issues. Their end-to-end model combines research, web search, file management, document management systems and drafting tools, while retaining human involvement at key decision points.
qs: End-to-end: agents can complete multi-step legal tasks from start to finish using a variety of tools.

From legal due diligence, to complex drafting, to long-running workflows using research, web search, file management, DMS, and drafting tools—while checking in with humans at key decision points along the way.
In practice, this means agents don't just review clauses—they redline the document.
They don't just suggest research angles—they compose and execute queries, synthesize results, and incorporate findings.
They don't just identify issues in a data room—they organize it, review it exhaustively and produce the diligence report.

kp.k: Legal deployment requires safeguards beyond frontier model capability
kp.d: The authors argue that frontier models alone cannot meet legal demands without domain knowledge, data, context, governance and oversight. They present matter grounding, structured human review, auditability, organization-wide controls and legal-specific tools as conditions for safe deployment at law-firm scale. These are vendor-stated platform characteristics and safety claims, not reported validation results.
qs: If deployed without legal-specific knowledge, data sources, context, governance, or oversight, even the best models can't meet the demands of real legal work.
Full matter context — every agent action is grounded in the client and matter context, the applicable playbooks, and the firm's knowledge and standards
Review and approval flows — humans stay in the loop at the points that matter, with structured checkpoints built into every workflow
Complete audit trails — every action an agent takes is traceable, reviewable, and defensible
Enterprise governance — standardized workflows that can be deployed, managed, and controlled across an entire organization, balancing performance and risk management.
Legal-specific tools — purpose-built tooling for how legal work actually gets done, from tabular review, to DMS integrations, to redlining to research

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Adrian Parlow and Ryan Wilson predict that 2026 marks the transition from assistive legal AI to agents executing complex legal work end-to-end, with human oversight.
pts.d: The Legora authors describe legal AI as following software development's trajectory one cycle behind: basic document question-answering in 2023, advanced multi-step workflows in 2025, and autonomous end-to-end execution in 2026. They distinguish agents, which plan, act, evaluate results and adapt until completion, from both question-answering chatbots and predetermined chains of prompts. Their claim concerns task execution with built-in human checkpoints, not entirely unsupervised legal practice.

pts.k: Parlow and Wilson claim that agents enable matter-wide review, multi-tool execution and persistent personalization, rather than merely suggesting legal work.
pts.d: The authors identify three capabilities: working across an entire matter file, completing multi-step tasks using research and document-management tools, and retaining drafting positions and client preferences across sessions. They claim exhaustive review beyond the scale of any human team and describe agents producing redlines, incorporating research findings and generating diligence reports. These are presented as capabilities of the emerging agent category; the article does not document a specific completed legal deployment for each example.

pts.k: Parlow and Wilson argue that frontier models alone cannot support real legal work and that purpose-built legal platforms supply the controls needed for deployment at scale.
pts.d: The authors attribute safe, scalable deployment to matter context, legal knowledge and tools, structured human review and approval, audit trails and enterprise governance. They present Legora as providing these elements and distinguish it from a frontier model with a legal plug-in. This is their platform and risk-management claim, rather than a reported independent finding about safety.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The main basis offered is an analogy to software-agent progress, a structural comparison of legal and software work, and the authors' descriptions of their platform.
pts.d: Parlow and Wilson cite a progression from GitHub Copilot's line completion to Cursor's file editing and Claude Code's autonomous multi-hour tasks. They identify Claude Opus 4.5 as a capability inflection point and assert that AI can more reliably complete software tasks taking humans 12 hours. The supplied text includes a '(source)' marker for that claim and another for the READ–THINK–WRITE–VERIFY workflow model, but supplies neither underlying source details nor results. Their transfer argument rests on both domains being text-intensive, precision-sensitive, iterative and dependent on large context and reusable patterns. No legal benchmark scores, measured legal error rates, client case results or quantified productivity outcomes are provided. Legora's feature descriptions and the Walter AI announcement support the authors' account of what they are building, rather than an independent evaluation of its outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The prediction is explicitly for 2026, while the March 11, 2026 article also says recent advances have already made the vision a reality.
pts.d: The authors combine a year-specific forecast with present-tense capability claims and statements that Legora and Walter AI are still building together. They do not give a narrower release date or adoption timetable. End-to-end execution is qualified by human intervention at key decisions; reliable deployment is conditioned on legal-specific context, data, tools, governance and oversight. Memory-driven personalization is expected to improve with repeated use across sessions. The article does not predict when all legal teams will adopt these systems.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The stated beneficiaries and users are legal teams and law firms, whose review, drafting, research and diligence workflows would shift toward delegated execution and human approval.
pts.d: The article explicitly references associates' contract-review work, law-firm deployment and organization-wide management of agent workflows. Lawyers would receive executed work products rather than only answers or suggestions, while retaining review and decision checkpoints. Firms would manage standardized workflows, auditability and risk controls; client context and preferences would inform outputs. Legora and Walter AI position themselves as vendors building this capability for customers. The authors do not specify effects on employment levels, associate hiring, staffing leverage, legal fees, access to justice or market shares, and do not separately forecast effects for in-house departments or particular firm sizes.
